Juvenile Yellowtail barracuda (Sphyraena flavicauda) emerging from the pelagic larval phase begin exogenous feeding after complete yolk-sac resorption, a critical transition that depends on the availability of small zooplankton. The fertilised ovum itself is minute, with a diameter of approximately 1.45 millimeters, leading to a calculated wet weight at birth of approximately 0.0016 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.0016 grams] for the newly hatched yolk-sac larva. This initial mass is typical for teleosts producing pelagic eggs, as the yolk-laden egg must remain buoyant in the water column. Growth during the early larval stages is rapid, driven by high ingestion rates of copepod nauplii. The species exhibits a protracted spawning season in tropical waters, and the timing of first feeding is tightly linked to environmental productivity cycles. The yolk-dependent larva, or prolarva, relies entirely on endogenous reserves until the mouth gapes open and retinal differentiation allows prey detection. Survival through this period is highly variable and strongly density-independent, governed largely by stochastic encounters with prey patches. The delicate chorionate embryo develops swiftly, and eclosion typically occurs within 24 to 30 hours post-fertilisation under optimal thermal regimes.

Females of Sphyraena flavicauda attain sexual maturity upon reaching a fork length at puberty of 28 centimeters [Lp = 28 centimeters], a size that corresponds to a calculated wet weight at puberty of 121 grams [Wwp = 121 grams]. This size threshold is reached after approximately one to two years of growth in the tropical waters this species inhabits. The onset of gonadal maturation, including vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males, is triggered by a combination of day length and rising water temperatures. Histological examination of ovaries from captured specimens indicates that the first wave of oocyte development begins once individuals surpass this body size, ensuring that spawning adults have sufficient somatic reserves to support gamete production. Reaching 28 centimeters [Lp = 28 centimeters] fork length signals a major life-history transition from a rapidly growing juvenile to a reproductively viable organism. This length-based maturation schedule is consistent with patterns observed in other scombrid and barracuda species, where a minimum size is required before the HPG axis becomes fully active. Fully mature females are capable of producing multiple batches of eggs within a single spawning season, a strategy that maximises lifetime fecundity in an environment where larval survival is unpredictable.

Estimates of the maximum recorded body size in Yellowtail barracuda indicate it can achieve an ultimate fork length of 60 centimeters [Li = 60 centimeters], a dimension from which the corresponding ultimate wet weight is derived to be approximately 1,100 grams [Wwi = approximately 1,100 grams]. This asymptotic size represents the upper boundary of somatic growth in the species, beyond which further increases in length become negligible. Large adults of this size are relatively uncommon in coastal catches, suggesting that natural mortality or fishing pressure limits the number of individuals reaching this upper size class. The length-weight relationship used to calculate this mass from length data follows a standard power function typical of fusiform-bodied pelagic predators. An individual nearing this ultimate fork length (60 cm) [Li = 60 cm] is likely several years old and has survived the intense predation pressure that characterises early life stages. Such large adults occupy the apex of the nearshore food web, feeding on small schooling fishes like anchovies and sardines. Their body plan, including a streamlined shape and a large forked tail, is optimised for high-speed pursuit of prey in open water. The energetic demands of maintaining this large body mass are substantial.

Under controlled experimental conditions, female Yellowtail barracuda maintained at a water temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C] express their maximum reproductive output. This maximum reproductive rate arises from a combination of high fecundity per spawning event and frequent spawning intervals. Females produce approximately 700 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 700 eggs per clutch], and spawning occurs almost daily during the peak of the reproductive season, yielding approximately 1 spawning event per day [F_R_i = approximately 1 spawning event per day]. This near-daily spawning interval sets this species apart from most coastal scombroids, reflecting the continuous warm temperatures and abundant food resources available in equatorial environments. The cumulative annual output from such a strategy is enormous, allowing the species to rapidly colonise favourable habitats. The specific value for maximum daily egg production, a rate that exceeds those reported for most other scombrid species of comparable body size, was calculated at a stable temperature of 27.7 °C [T = 27.7 °C], highlighting the sensitivity of reproductive physiology to thermal conditions. If water temperatures deviate significantly from this optimum, spawning frequency and clutch size both decline, reducing overall recruitment potential for that year. This thermal dependency links the species' reproductive success directly to seasonal and interannual climate variability in its range.

Longevity records for Sphyraena flavicauda, derived from otolith annulus counts and mark-recapture studies, indicate a maximum lifespan of 12 years [am = 12 years] for individuals inhabiting waters with a mean annual temperature near 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C]. This lifespan is moderate for a fish of its body size, falling within the range observed for many tropical scombrids and barracudas and is consistent with the maximum longevity reported for other barracuda species in the genus Sphyraena. The age-structured mortality patterns suggest that senescence-related declines in swimming performance and feeding efficiency become apparent after approximately a decade. The constant temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C] under which these longevity estimates were obtained reflects the stable thermal environment of the core tropical Indo-Pacific range of this species, where seasonal fluctuations are minimal. In cooler peripheral populations, metabolic rates are lower, potentially extending lifespan slightly, though growth rates also decline. A 12-year-old individual (12 years) [am = 12 years] will have contributed multiple spawning seasons to the population, reinforcing the importance of large, old females as the primary drivers of reproductive output in this iteroparous species at a temperature of 28.4 °C [T = 28.4 °C].
